claim: Human genetic studies have emphasised the dominant contribution of pancreatic islet dysfunction to development of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D).
source: Human genetic studies have emphasised the dominant contribution of pancreatic islet dysfunction to development of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the broader scientific literature and context of the study.

claim: The study characterised patterns of chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq, n = 17) in human islets.
source: We characterised patterns of chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq, n = 17) and DNA methylation (whole-genome bisulphite sequencing, n = 10) in human islets, generating high-resolution chromatin state maps through integration with established ChIP-seq marks.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methods and sample sizes used in the study.

claim: The study characterised patterns of DNA methylation (whole-genome bisulphite sequencing, n = 10) in human islets.
source: We characterised patterns of chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq, n = 17) and DNA methylation (whole-genome bisulphite sequencing, n = 10) in human islets, generating high-resolution chromatin state maps through integration with established ChIP-seq marks.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methods and sample sizes used in the study.

claim: Enrichment of GWAS signals for T2D and fasting glucose was concentrated in subsets of islet enhancers characterised by open chromatin and hypomethylation.
source: We found enrichment of GWAS signals for T2D and fasting glucose was concentrated in subsets of islet enhancers characterised by open chromatin and hypomethylation, with the former annotation predominant.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the integration of GWAS data with epigenomic annotations.

claim: Open chromatin annotation was predominant over hypomethylation for enrichment of GWAS signals.
source: We found enrichment of GWAS signals for T2D and fasting glucose was concentrated in subsets of islet enhancers characterised by open chromatin and hypomethylation, with the former annotation predominant.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the study's analysis of different epigenomic features.

claim: At CDC123, ADCY5, and KLHDC5 loci, the combination of fine-mapping genetic data and chromatin state enrichment maps pinpointed likely causal variants.
source: At several loci (including CDC123, ADCY5, KLHDC5) the combination of fine-mapping genetic data and chromatin state enrichment maps, supplemented by allelic imbalance in chromatin accessibility pinpointed likely causal variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on integrative analysis of genetic and epigenomic data.

claim: Allelic imbalance in chromatin accessibility supplemented the identification of likely causal variants at CDC123, ADCY5, and KLHDC5 loci.
source: At several loci (including CDC123, ADCY5, KLHDC5) the combination of fine-mapping genetic data and chromatin state enrichment maps, supplemented by allelic imbalance in chromatin accessibility pinpointed likely causal variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Recent GWAS have identified a large number of T2D susceptibility loci.
source: Recent GWAS have identified a large number of T2D susceptibility loci (Scott et al., 2017; Mahajan et al., 2014; Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al., 2012; Voight et al., 2010), the majority of which affect insulin secretion and beta cell function (Dimas et al., 2014; Wood et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published GWAS studies.

claim: The majority of T2D susceptibility loci affect insulin secretion and beta cell function.
source: Recent GWAS have identified a large number of T2D susceptibility loci (Scott et al., 2017; Mahajan et al., 2014; Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al., 2012; Voight et al., 2010), the majority of which affect insulin secretion and beta cell function (Dimas et al., 2014; Wood et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Most GWAS signals map to the non-coding genome.
source: However, most GWAS signals map to the non-coding genome and identification of the molecular mechanisms through which non-coding variants exert their effect has proven challenging.
evidence: This is a general observation about GWAS findings supported by the broader literature.

claim: T2D-associated variants map disproportionately to regulatory elements, particularly those which influence RNA expression and cellular function of human pancreatic islets.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that T2D-associated variants map disproportionately to regulatory elements, particularly those which influence RNA expression and cellular function of human pancreatic islets. (Parker et al., 2013; Pasquali et al., 2014; van de Bunt et al., 2015; Olsson et al., 2014; Dayeh et al., 2014; Volkov et al., 2017; Varshney et al., 2017; Gaulton et al., 2015, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The use of DNA methylation and open chromatin data to further annotate ChIP-seq derived chromatin states has successfully uncovered novel biology for other diseases.
source: The use of DNA methylation and open chromatin data to further annotate ChIP-seq derived chromatin states has successfully uncovered novel biology for other diseases (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Existing methylation studies in islets have either profiled a very small proportion of methylation sites using methylation arrays or focused on T2D-associated disease differentially methylated regions rather than the integration of DNA methylation status with T2D-relevant GWAS data.
source: Existing methylation studies in islets, however, have either profiled a very small proportion of methylation sites using methylation arrays (Olsson et al., 2014; Dayeh et al., 2014) or focused on T2D-associated disease differentially methylated regions (dDMRs) rather than the integration of DNA methylation status with T2D-relevant GWAS data (Volkov et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies and describes limitations of prior work.

claim: Assays of open chromatin in human islets have been restricted to small sample numbers.
source: At the same time, assays of open chromatin in human islets have been restricted to small sample numbers (limiting the potential to capture allelic imbalance in chromatin accessibility for example): these have focussed predominantly on the impact of clustered or 'stretch' enhancers (Parker et al., 2013; Pasquali et al., 2014; Gaulton et al., 2010; Varshney et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies and describes limitations of prior work.

claim: Reference annotations of the islet epigenome and transcriptome have been largely absent from projects such as GTEx, ENCODE and Epigenome Roadmap.
source: Most importantly, in part due to historical challenges in accessing human islet material or authentic human cellular models, reference annotations of the islet epigenome and transcriptome (in the context of projects such as GTEx, ENCODE and Epigenome Roadmap) have been largely absent.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field and available resources.

claim: Islets constitute only ~1% of the pancreas.
source: It is worth noting that islets constitute only ~1% of the pancreas, and islet epigenomes and transcriptomes cannot therefore be reliably assayed in analyses involving the entire organ.
evidence: This is a statement of biological fact.

claim: Islet epigenomes and transcriptomes cannot be reliably assayed in analyses involving the entire pancreas organ.
source: It is worth noting that islets constitute only ~1% of the pancreas, and islet epigenomes and transcriptomes cannot therefore be reliably assayed in analyses involving the entire organ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low proportion of islets in the pancreas.

claim: WGBS was performed with mean coverage of 13X in human pancreatic islet DNA samples isolated from 10 non-diabetic cadaveric donors of European descent.
source: To characterise the human islet methylome and characterise the role of DNA methylation with respect to T2D genetic risk, we performed WGBS (mean coverage 13X) in human pancreatic islet DNA samples isolated from 10 non-diabetic cadaveric donors of European descent.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and sample characteristics.

claim: Methylation levels across the genome were highly correlated across individual donors (mean CpG methylation Spearman's rho across 10 individual WGBS donors = 0.71).
source: Methylation levels across the genome were highly correlated across individual donors (mean CpG methylation Spearman's rho across 10 individual WGBS donors = 0.71, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A): we pooled the WGBS results to generate a single high-pass (mean coverage 85X) set of pooled human pancreatic islet methylation data covering 23.3 million CpG sites (minimum pooled coverage 10X).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Pooled WGBS results generated a single high-pass (mean coverage 85X) set of pooled human pancreatic islet methylation data covering 23.3 million CpG sites (minimum pooled coverage 10X).
source: Methylation levels across the genome were highly correlated across individual donors (mean CpG methylation Spearman's rho across 10 individual WGBS donors = 0.71, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A): we pooled the WGBS results to generate a single high-pass (mean coverage 85X) set of pooled human pancreatic islet methylation data covering 23.3 million CpG sites (minimum pooled coverage 10X).
evidence: This describes the data processing and resulting coverage.

claim: 450k array methylation data was generated from 32 islet samples ascertained from non-diabetic donors of European descent.
source: For comparative purposes, we generated 450 k array methylation data from 32 islet samples ascertained from non-diabetic donors of European descent (five overlapping with those from whom WGBS data were generated).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and sample characteristics.

claim: Methylation levels were highly correlated across individuals for 450k array data (mean CpG methylation Spearman's rho across 32 individual 450k donor = 0.98).
source: As with the WGBS data, methylation levels were highly correlated across individuals (mean CpG methylation Spearman's rho across 32 individual 450 k donor = 0.98, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Methylation profiles generated from the 450k array and WGBS were highly correlated at overlapping CpG sites (pooled WGBS vs. 450k Spearman's rho = 0.89).
source: After pooling 450 k array data across samples, methylation profiles generated from the 450 k array and WGBS were highly correlated at the small subset of total CpG sites for which they overlap: this was observed across pooled samples (pooled WGBS vs. 450 k Spearman's rho = 0.89, Figure 1A) and across the five donors analysed by both methods (mean Spearman's rho = 0.80, not shown).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The 450k array was designed to interrogate approximately 2% of all CpG sites in the genome (~480k CpG sites).
source: WGBS and 450 k array data differed substantially in terms of genome-wide coverage. The 450 k array was designed to interrogate with high precision and coverage ~480 k CpG sites (approximately 2% of all sites in the genome), selected primarily because they are located near gene promoters and CpG-island regions.
evidence: This describes the design characteristics of the 450k array.

claim: The 450k array CpG sites were selected primarily because they are located near gene promoters and CpG-island regions.
source: The 450 k array was designed to interrogate with high precision and coverage ~480 k CpG sites (approximately 2% of all sites in the genome), selected primarily because they are located near gene promoters and CpG-island regions.
evidence: This describes the design characteristics of the 450k array.

claim: WGBS data revealed widespread high methylation levels with hypomethylation (<50%) restricted to 11.2% (2.6M/23.3M CpG sites) of the genome.
source: Whilst the WGBS data revealed the expected pattern of widespread high methylation levels with hypomethylation (<50%) restricted to 11.2% (2.6M/23.3M CpG sites) of the genome, the array disproportionately interrogated those hypomethylated sites (218 k [46%] of all 450 k CpG probes) (Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test for difference, D = 0.40, p<2.2×10−16) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The 450k array disproportionately interrogated hypomethylated sites (218k [46%] of all 450k CpG probes).
source: Whilst the WGBS data revealed the expected pattern of widespread high methylation levels with hypomethylation (<50%) restricted to 11.2% (2.6M/23.3M CpG sites) of the genome, the array disproportionately interrogated those hypomethylated sites (218 k [46%] of all 450 k CpG probes) (Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test for difference, D = 0.40, p<2.2×10−16) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical test.

claim: Significant differences were found between the methylation levels of CpG sites accessed on the 450k array and those interrogated by WGBS across most islet chromatin states (FDR < 0.05).
source: We found significant (FDR < 0.05) differences between the methylation levels of CpG sites accessed on the array, and those interrogated by WGBS, across most islet chromatin states: the largest differences were observed for weak promoters (median WGBS = 0.71 vs. median 450k = 0.11, KS test D = 0.51, p<2.2×10−16,) and weak enhancers (WGBS = 0.87 vs. 450 k median = 0.76, D = 0.39, p<2.2×10−16, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: The 450k array assayed only ~2.9% of CpG sites in strong enhancer states.
source: In terms of coverage, most chromatin states, apart from promoters, were poorly represented by CpG sites directly interrogated by the array: for example the array assayed only ~2.9% of CpG sites in strong enhancer states (2.7–3.8% depending on strong enhancer subtype, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Methylation levels are highly correlated across short (0.1–2 kb) genomic distances.
source: Although methylation levels were previously reported to be highly correlated across short (0.1–2 kb) genomic distances (Zhang et al., 2015; Bell et al., 2011; Eckhardt et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2017), the observed significant differences in the methylation distribution (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) across chromatin states including weak promoter (median size 600 bp) and enhancer subtypes (median size ranges from 200 to 1200 bp) indicate that these correlative effects are not strong enough to counterbalance the low coverage of the 450 k array.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The 450k array has limited capacity to comprehensively interrogate the global DNA methylome, particularly at distal regulatory states such as enhancers.
source: These findings are consistent with 450 k array content being focused towards CpG-dense hypomethylated and permissive promoter regions. This highlights the limited capacity of the array to comprehensively interrogate the global DNA methylome, in particular at distal regulatory states such as enhancers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis showing differences in coverage and methylation distributions.

claim: The DIAGRAM GWAS dataset involved 26.7k cases and 132.5k controls of predominantly European origin.
source: We used the largest currently available T2D DIAGRAM GWAS data set (involving 26.7 k cases and 132.5 k controls of predominantly European origin, see dataset section for details) to identify the 'credible sets' of variants at each locus which collectively account for 99% of the posterior probability of association (PPA) (Scott et al., 2017; Maller et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the GWAS dataset used in the study.

claim: Coverage of T2D GWAS variants by the 450k array is low, with a median PPA per locus of 16%.
source: We found that coverage of this space of putative T2D GWAS variants by the 450 k array is low: across GWAS loci, the combined PPA attributable to variants within regions assayed by the array ranged from 0–99% with a median PPA per locus of 16% (compared to a WGBS median PPA per locus = 99%, KS-test p<2.2×10−16, Figure 1D, top).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical test.

claim: WGBS has a median PPA per locus of 99% for T2D GWAS variants.
source: We found that coverage of this space of putative T2D GWAS variants by the 450 k array is low: across GWAS loci, the combined PPA attributable to variants within regions assayed by the array ranged from 0–99% with a median PPA per locus of 16% (compared to a WGBS median PPA per locus = 99%, KS-test p<2.2×10−16, Figure 1D, top).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical test.

claim: The 850k array would capture approximately 39% of the PPA for T2D GWAS variants (range 0%–99%).
source: We estimated that the equivalent figure for a recently developed upgrade of the 450 k array, which captures ~850 k CpG sites and aims to provide better coverage of enhancer regions, would be ~39% (range 0%–99% Figure 1D, top).
evidence: This is an estimate based on analysis of the 850k array manifest.

claim: At the DGKB T2D locus, CpG sites covered by the 450k array interrogated less than 1% of the PPA of associated variants.
source: For instance, at the DGKB T2D locus (centred on rs10276674), CpG sites covered by the 450 k array interrogated less than 1% of the PPA of associated variants (vs. 99% captured by WGBS); the figure for the 850 k array would be 23% (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a specific example from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: At the DGKB T2D locus, WGBS captured 99% of the PPA of associated variants.
source: For instance, at the DGKB T2D locus (centred on rs10276674), CpG sites covered by the 450 k array interrogated less than 1% of the PPA of associated variants (vs. 99% captured by WGBS); the figure for the 850 k array would be 23% (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a specific example from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Hypomethylation is a strong indicator of regulatory function.
source: Studies in a variety of other tissues have shown that hypomethylation is a strong indicator of regulatory function (Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Low-Methylated Regions (LMRs) with methylation ranging from 10–50% and containing fewer than 30 CpG sites denote potential distal regulatory elements such as enhancers.
source: More specifically, continuous stretches of CpG-poor Low-Methylated Regions (LMRs, with methylation ranging from 10–50% and containing fewer than 30 CpG sites) denote potential distal regulatory elements such as enhancers, while stretches of CpG-rich UnMethylated Regions (UMRs, containing more than 30 CpG sites) are more likely to represent proximal regulatory elements including promoters (Burger et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: UnMethylated Regions (UMRs) containing more than 30 CpG sites are more likely to represent proximal regulatory elements including promoters.
source: More specifically, continuous stretches of CpG-poor Low-Methylated Regions (LMRs, with methylation ranging from 10–50% and containing fewer than 30 CpG sites) denote potential distal regulatory elements such as enhancers, while stretches of CpG-rich UnMethylated Regions (UMRs, containing more than 30 CpG sites) are more likely to represent proximal regulatory elements including promoters (Burger et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The study detected 37.1k LMRs, 13.6k UMRs, and 10.7k PMDs.
source: We detected 37.1 k LMRs, 13.6 k UMRs (Figure 2A) and 10.7 k Partially Methylated Domains (PMDs) (Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: 69.2% of islet LMRs overlapped islet strong and weak enhancer states.
source: As anticipated, we found significant enrichment of LMRs with weak and strong enhancer states as defined by islet chromatin state maps derived from existing ChIP-seq data (Parker et al., 2013) (69.2% of islet LMRs overlapped islet strong and weak enhancer states, log2FE = 2.2–2.9, Bonferroni p<0.05, Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to figures and statistical tests.

claim: 90.8% of UMRs overlapped islet active promoters.
source: Similarly, UMRs were enriched for islet active promoter chromatin states (90.8% of UMRs overlapped islet active promoters, log2FE = 3.9, Bonferroni p < 0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: LMRs showed marked enrichment for eQTLs (LMR log2FE = 1.1, UMR log2FE = 2.7, Bonferroni p<0.05).
source: We observed marked enrichment for eQTLs (LMR log2FE = 1.1, UMR log2FE = 2.7, Bonferroni p<0.05) and TFBS (LMR log2FE = 4.1–4.6; UMR log2FE = 2.4–3.9, Bonferroni p<0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: LMRs and UMRs showed marked enrichment for TFBS (LMR log2FE = 4.1–4.6; UMR log2FE = 2.4–3.9, Bonferroni p<0.05).
source: We observed marked enrichment for eQTLs (LMR log2FE = 1.1, UMR log2FE = 2.7, Bonferroni p<0.05) and TFBS (LMR log2FE = 4.1–4.6; UMR log2FE = 2.4–3.9, Bonferroni p<0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: Islet LMRs and UMRs correspond to important tissue-specific regulatory regions.
source: These observations confirm that islet LMRs and UMRs correspond to important tissue-specific regulatory regions, overlapping cis-regulatory annotations known to be enriched for T2D GWAS signals (Pasquali et al., 2014; Gaulton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment data and supported by citations.

claim: Only 2.2% of dDMRs overlapped LMRs and 2.4% overlapped UMRs.
source: We found only limited overlap between these dDMRs and the UMRs and LMRs from our data: of the 25,820 dDMRs, 2.2% overlapped LMRs and 2.4% UMRs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: The overlap between dDMRs and LMRs/UMRs was slightly greater than expected by chance (Bonferroni p<0.05, LMR log2FE = 1.0 and promoter-like UMRs log2FE = 1.1).
source: This overlap was slightly greater than expected by chance (Bonferroni p<0.05, LMR log2FE = 1.0 and promoter-like UMRs log2FE = 1.1, Figure 2B) but more modest than seen for the other regulatory annotations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: dDMRs showed modest (log2FE = 0.4–1.0) but significant (Bonferroni p<0.05) levels of enrichment with respect to all other islet regulatory annotations.
source: Similarly, we also observed that dDMRs showed more modest (log2FE = 0.4–1.0), but still significant (Bonferroni p<0.05) levels of enrichment with respect to all other islet regulatory annotations (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure and statistical tests.

claim: Only a fraction of dDMRs correspond to islet genomic regulatory sites.
source: The modest enrichment of dDMRs indicates that only a fraction of these regions correspond to islet genomic regulatory sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modest enrichment data.

claim: Most dDMRs are unlikely to directly contribute to the mediation of genetic T2D risk.
source: Given that T2D risk variants preferentially map in islet regulatory sites, the corollary is that most dDMRs are unlikely to directly contribute to the mediation of genetic T2D risk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modest enrichment data and the known preference of T2D risk variants for regulatory sites.

claim: The study identified a total of 141k open chromatin regions based on read depth, peak width and signal-to-noise ratio.
source: We identified a total of 141 k open chromatin regions based on read depth, peak width and signal-to-noise ratio (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: 78% of islet open chromatin regions showed substantial overlap with equivalent regions described in a recent study of two human islets.
source: These regions of islet open chromatin showed substantial overlap (78%) with equivalent regions described in a recent study of two human islets (Varshney et al., 2017) (log2FE = 2.8 compared to random sites, not shown).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis and comparison with published data.

claim: 53% of LMRs overlapped 16% of all ATAC-seq peaks (LMR log2FE = 3.8 compared to randomised sites).
source: In addition, our islet ATAC-Seq sites demonstrated substantial overlap with LMRs: 53% of LMRs overlapped 16% of all ATAC-seq peaks (LMR log2FE = 3.8 compared to randomised sites, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Almost all UMRs (98%) were contained within regions overlapping (13% of) ATAC-seq peaks (UMR log2FE = 3.4 compared to randomised sites).
source: Almost all UMRs (98%) were contained within regions overlapping (13% of) ATAC-seq peaks (UMR log2FE = 3.4 compared to randomised sites, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The augmented chromatin state maps generated 15 islet chromatin states using chromHMM.
source: To fully leverage information across multiple overlapping islet epigenome assays, we generated augmented chromatin state maps, using chromHMM (Ernst and Kellis, 2012). These maps combined the WGBS methylation and ATAC-Seq open chromatin data with previously generated ChIP-seq marks (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the computational method used to generate chromatin state maps, with reference to figures.

claim: The augmented chromatin state maps identified two subclasses of strong enhancers: 'open' (n = 32k genome-wide) and 'closed' (n = 110k).
source: The addition of islet methylation and open chromatin data expanded existing chromatin state definitions to provide new subclasses, particularly amongst enhancer elements. Here, we observed two subclasses of strong enhancers and three of weak enhancers (Figure 3A). We denote the strong enhancer subtypes as 'open' (n = 32 k genome-wide), characterised by open chromatin and hypomethylation, and 'closed' (n = 110 k) with closed chromatin and hypermethylation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the chromatin state analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The augmented chromatin state maps identified three subclasses of weak enhancers: 'open' (n = 38k), 'lowly-methylated' (n = 78k), and 'closed' (n = 206k).
source: The three weak enhancer states we denote as 'open' (n = 38k: open chromatin, hypomethylation), 'lowly-methylated' (n = 78 k; closed chromatin, hypomethylation) and 'closed' (n = 206k: closed chromatin, hypermethylation).
evidence: This is a result from the chromatin state analysis.

claim: There was considerable overlap between the 'open' strong and weak enhancer states and previously-described 'stretch' enhancer states (16.1k out of 23k stretch enhancer overlapped 32k out of 70.1k 'open' enhancers).
source: Additional comparison to 'stretch' enhancer clusters (Parker et al., 2013), showed that there was considerable overlap between the 'open' strong and weak enhancer states we identify here and previously-described 'stretch' enhancer states (16.1 k out of 23 k stretch enhancer overlapped 32 k out of 70.1 k 'open' enhancers).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis comparing with published data.

claim: Most (55%) 'open' enhancer states were not captured within 'stretch' enhancer intervals.
source: Even so, most (55%) 'open' enhancer states, and in particular 'open weak enhancers' (70%), were not captured within 'stretch' enhancer intervals, and we regard these as distinct islet enhancer subclasses.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: In single-feature FGWAS analyses, significant enrichment was limited to four enhancer states (open weak enhancers, both types of strong enhancer and H3K36me3 marked genic enhancers).
source: In single-feature analyses, we found significant enrichment (lower limit of Confidence Interval (CI) >0) limited to four enhancer states (open weak enhancers, both types of strong enhancer and H3K36me3 marked genic enhancers) (Figure 3B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure and table.

claim: FGWAS multi-feature analyses for T2D retained both subclasses of strong enhancer, the subclass of open weak enhancers, genic enhancers and CDS in the joint model.
source: FGWAS multi-feature analyses for T2D, incorporating all annotations positive in single-element analyses, retained both subclasses of strong enhancer, the subclass of open weak enhancers, genic enhancers and CDS in the joint model (Figure 3C and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Conserved sequence annotations were not retained in the FGWAS joint model for T2D.
source: Conserved sequence annotations were not retained in the joint model.
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis.

claim: Markedly different levels of enrichment for T2D association were observed between and within open and closed enhancer states.
source: We observed markedly different levels of enrichment for T2D association between and within open and closed enhancer states (Figure 3B–3C, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to figures and a table.

claim: Clear enrichment for T2D association was demonstrated for the subset of 'open' weak enhancers (12% of all weak enhancer sites) with no evidence of enrichment in the remaining subclasses.
source: Using these augmented chromatin state maps, we demonstrated clear enrichment for T2D association for the subset of 'open' weak enhancers (12% of all weak enhancer sites) with no evidence of enrichment in the remaining subclasses ('closed' and 'lowly-methylated') (Figure 3B and Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure and table.

claim: The most marked enrichment was amongst open strong enhancers (22% of the total).
source: We also saw differences in enrichment signal between open and closed strong enhancers, with the most marked enrichment amongst open strong enhancers (22% of the total, Figure 3B–C, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to figures and a table.

claim: In joint-analysis, open strong enhancers showed higher enrichment (joint log2FE = 4.1, CI = 3.3 to 4.8) than closed strong enhancers (joint log2FE = 2.4, CI = 0.5 to 3.3).
source: This effect was particularly obvious in the joint-analysis (open strong enhancer joint log2FE = 4.1, CI = 3.3 to 4.8 vs. closed strong enhancer joint log2FE = 2.4, CI = 0.5 to 3.3, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The T2D GWAS enrichment signal was predominantly driven by the distribution of islet open chromatin.
source: These analyses confirmed that the T2D GWAS enrichment signal was predominantly driven by the distribution of islet open chromatin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis comparing different chromatin state models, with reference to a figure.

claim: LMRs were significantly enriched (log2FE = 3.2, CI = 2.3 to 3.9) for T2D association signals.
source: LMRs were significantly (lower CI limit >0) enriched (log2FE = 3.2, CI = 2.3 to 3.9) for T2D association signals consistent with their co-localisation with distal regulatory elements, and displayed modestly increased enrichment compared to enhancer states derived from ChIP-seq alone (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: No significant enrichment was found for human islet UMRs (log2FE = 1.4, CI = −0.6 to 2.5) or PMDs (log2FE = −0.8, CI = −1.7 to −0.1) for T2D association.
source: In contrast, no significant enrichment was found for human islet (promoter-like) UMRs (log2FE = 1.4, CI = −0.6 to 2.5) or PMDs (log2FE = −0.8, CI = −1.7 to −0.1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis.

claim: There was no evidence that dDMRs were enriched for genome-wide T2D association signals (log2FE = −24.6, CI = −44.6 to 3.7).
source: We also found no evidence that recently-described regions of T2D-associated differential methylation (dDMRs: derived from comparison of WGBS data from islets of diabetic and non-diabetic individuals) were enriched for genome-wide T2D association signals (log2FE = −24.6, CI = −44.6 to 3.7) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The improvement in enrichment was mainly driven by open chromatin but LMRs also contributed significantly and independently.
source: This confirmed that the improvement in enrichment was mainly driven by open chromatin but showed that LMRs also contributed significantly and independently to the enrichment (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from the nested model FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: FGWAS analysis for FG corroborated the observations from T2D analysis.
source: FGWAS analysis for FG corroborated the observations from T2D analysis. Despite reduced power of the FG GWAS data due to a lower number of significantly associated FG GWAS loci, both single feature and joint-model analyses of human islet epigenome data found significant enrichment in strong enhancer states with the strongest enrichment in enhancers with open chromatin and hypomethylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B and Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis for FG, with reference to figures and a table.

claim: Open chromatin was primarily responsible for the enhanced enrichment in FG GWAS analysis.
source: In addition, evaluation of the relative contributions of ATAC-seq open chromatin and DNA methylation to FG GWAS enrichment across both single-feature (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D) and joint-model analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F and Figure 3—source data 3) indicated that open chromatin was primarily responsible for the enhanced enrichment.
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis for FG, with reference to figures.

claim: The addition of open chromatin and DNA methylation data to ChIP-seq marks enhances the resolution of regulatory annotation for human islets.
source: Overall, these analyses demonstrate that the addition of open chromatin and DNA methylation data to ChIP-seq marks enhances the resolution of regulatory annotation for human islets.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the FGWAS enrichment analyses.

claim: The addition of open chromatin and DNA methylation data defines subsets of weak and strong enhancers that differ markedly with respect to the impact of genetic variation on T2D risk.
source: In particular, it defines subsets of weak and strong enhancers that differ markedly with respect to the impact of genetic variation on T2D risk.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the FGWAS enrichment analyses.

claim: The effects of DNA accessibility predominate over hypomethylation status for T2D GWAS enrichment.
source: Although DNA accessibility and hypomethylation status are strongly correlated and provide broadly similar enrichments, the effects of the former predominate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the FGWAS enrichment analyses.

claim: T2D risk in relation to methylation status is primarily invested in hypomethylated LMRs (i.e. enhancers) rather than UMRs, dDMRs or PMDs.
source: In line with the dominance of open chromatin status for T2D GWAS enrichment, we observed that T2D risk in relation to methylation status is primarily invested in hypomethylated LMRs (i.e. enhancers) rather than UMRs, dDMRs or PMDs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the FGWAS enrichment analyses.

claim: FGWAS was applied to T2D DIAGRAM GWAS data under the joint model derived from the augmented chromatin state maps.
source: Specifically, we applied FGWAS to the T2D DIAGRAM GWAS data (Scott et al., 2017) under the joint model (Figure 3C) derived from the augmented chromatin state maps.
evidence: This describes the method used for fine-mapping analysis.

claim: The genome was divided into 2327 segments (average size 5004 SNPs or 1.2 Mb) for FGWAS analysis.
source: We divided the genome into 2327 segments (average size 5004 SNPs or 1.2 Mb) and identified 52 segments significantly associated with T2D genome-wide (segmental FGWAS PPA >= 0.9 or single variant GWAS p<5×10−8, see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the method used for FGWAS analysis.

claim: 52 segments were identified as significantly associated with T2D genome-wide (segmental FGWAS PPA >= 0.9 or single variant GWAS p<5×10−8).
source: We divided the genome into 2327 segments (average size 5004 SNPs or 1.2 Mb) and identified 52 segments significantly associated with T2D genome-wide (segmental FGWAS PPA >= 0.9 or single variant GWAS p<5×10−8, see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis.

claim: The 52 segments corresponded to 49 known T2D associated regions.
source: These corresponded to 49 known T2D associated regions representing that subset of the ~120 known T2D GWAS loci which passed those significance/filtering criteria in this European-only dataset.
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis.

claim: Analyses using enrichments from the augmented chromatin state model were associated with smaller 99% credible sets (median of 17 SNPs) than those derived from ChIP-seq data alone (median 23).
source: Consistent with the increased T2D GWAS enrichment of states including open chromatin and DNA methylation information, we found that analyses using enrichments from the augmented chromatin state model (combining ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and WGBS data) were associated with smaller 99% credible sets (median of 17 SNPs) than those derived from FGWAS enrichment derived from ChIP-seq data alone (median 23).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis comparing different models.

claim: The PPA for the best variant per locus increased with the augmented chromatin state model (median 0.39 vs 0.31 for ChIP-seq alone).
source: In parallel, the PPA for the best variant per locus increased (median 0.39 vs 0.31).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis comparing different models.

claim: The reduction in 99% credible set size and increase in maximum variant PPA was driven predominantly by open chromatin.
source: We also expanded the FGWAS PPA analysis to investigate open chromatin and DNA methylation effects on fine-mapping and found that the reduction in 99% credible set size and increase in maximum variant PPA was driven predominantly by open chromatin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The inclusion of open chromatin maps helps to improve prioritisation of causal variants at many T2D GWAS loci.
source: This demonstrates that the inclusion of open chromatin maps helps to improve prioritisation of causal variants at many T2D GWAS loci.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FGWAS analysis results.

claim: At 11 of 15 loci most clearly associated with deficient insulin secretion, islet 'open strong enhancer' states captured more than 60% of the PPA (median 92%).
source: At 11 of these 15 loci, we found that islet 'open strong enhancer' states, and to a lesser extent 'open weak enhancer' and 'closed strong enhancer', captured more than 60% of the PPA (median 92%, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Variants in islet enhancer subclasses captured at least 95% of the PPA at 4 T2D GWAS loci that have been previously implicated in human islet genome or functional regulation.
source: Variants in these islet enhancer subclasses also captured at least 95% of the PPA at 4 T2D GWAS loci that could not be classified according to physiological association data but which have been previously implicated in human islet genome or functional regulation based on islet eQTL (van de Bunt et al., 2015) or mQTL (Olsson et al., 2014) data (Figure 4C, genes highlighted in bold).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure and citations.

claim: At 3/6 of the insulin resistance and all but five unclassified loci, the PPA was mostly (>50%) attributable to other non-islet enhancer states.
source: In contrast, at 3/6 of the insulin resistance and all but five unclassified loci, the PPA was mostly (>50%) attributable to other non-islet enhancer states (across all insulin resistance and unclassified loci, DNA not overlapping islet enhancers and defined as 'Other' capture a median PPA of 64%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the FGWAS analysis.

claim: Islet regulatory annotations are particularly useful for fine-mapping T2D GWAS loci that affect insulin secretion and beta-cell function.
source: Thus, islet regulatory annotations are particularly useful for fine-mapping T2D GWAS loci that affect insulin secretion and beta-cell function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FGWAS analysis results.

claim: 54 variants within 33 T2D-associated GWAS segments were selected for testing of allelic imbalance based on reweighted variant PPA >= 10% and overlap with an enriched regulatory state.
source: We selected 54 variants within 33 T2D-associated GWAS segments for testing of allelic imbalance on the basis of (a) a reweighted variant PPA >= 10% and (b) overlap with an enriched regulatory state within the FGWAS T2D joint-model (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This describes the method for selecting variants for allelic imbalance testing.

claim: 20 variants (at 16 loci) had sufficient numbers of heterozygous samples (>2) and ATAC-seq read depth (depth >9 and at least five reads for each allele) for allelic imbalance testing.
source: Of these, 20 variants (at 16 loci) had sufficient numbers of heterozygous samples (>2) and ATAC-seq read depth (depth >9 and at least five reads for each allele).
evidence: This describes the filtering criteria for allelic imbalance testing.

claim: The strongest evidence for allelic imbalance (FDR < 0.05) was observed at 3 out of the 20 variants (rs11257655 near CDC123 and CAMK1D, rs10842991 near KLHDC5 and rs11708067 at ADCY5).
source: After correcting for mapping bias using WASP, we observed the strongest evidence for allelic imbalance (FDR < 0.05) at 3 out of the 20 variants (rs11257655 near CDC123 and CAMK1D, rs10842991 near KLHDC5 and rs11708067 at ADCY5) (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the allelic imbalance analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: All three variants showing allelic imbalance overlapped refined islet open strong or open weak enhancer regions characterised by open chromatin and hypomethylation.
source: All three overlapped refined islet open strong or open weak enhancer regions characterised by open chromatin and hypomethylation.
evidence: This is a result from the allelic imbalance analysis.

claim: Variant rs11257655 accounts for 95% of the reweighted PPA at the CDC123/CAMK1D locus.
source: Variant rs11257655 accounts for 95% of the reweighted PPA (compared to a PPA of 20% from genetic data alone) at the CDC123/CAMK1D locus, overlaps an 'open strong enhancer' region (Figure 5A) and the risk allele correlates with increased chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS and allelic imbalance analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: At rs11257655, the risk allele correlates with increased chromatin accessibility.
source: Variant rs11257655 accounts for 95% of the reweighted PPA (compared to a PPA of 20% from genetic data alone) at the CDC123/CAMK1D locus, overlaps an 'open strong enhancer' region (Figure 5A) and the risk allele correlates with increased chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is a result from the allelic imbalance analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: rs11257655 is in high LD (r2 = 0.82) with the lead variant for a cis-eQTL for CAMK1D in islets.
source: The same variant is in high LD (r2 = 0.82) with the lead variant for a cis-eQTL for CAMK1D in islets (van de Bunt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from the study's analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: In experimental assays, the T2D-risk allele of rs11257655 has been shown to be associated with increased CAMK1D gene expression and enhanced binding of the FOXA1 and FOXA2 transcription factors.
source: In experimental assays (Fogarty et al., 2014), the T2D-risk allele has been shown to be associated with increased CAMK1D gene expression and enhanced binding of the FOXA1 and FOXA2 transcription factors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: rs11257655 is the causal variant at the CDC123/CAMK1D locus.
source: These data all point to rs11257655 as the causal variant at this locus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of multiple lines of evidence.

claim: At KLHDC5, the credible set contained 23 variants in high mutual LD (r2 >0.8, top variant PPA <5%).
source: At KLHDC5, no clear causal variant emerged based on genetic fine-mapping data alone as the credible set contained 23 variants in high mutual LD (r2 >0.8, top variant PPA <5%, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the genetic fine-mapping analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: At KLHDC5, variants rs10771372, rs10842992 and rs10842991 overlapped 'open strong enhancer' regions.
source: Of these, variants rs10771372 (genetic fine-mapping PPA = 5%), rs10842992 (genetic fine mapping PPA = 5%) and rs10842991 (genetic fine-mapping PPA = 3%) overlapped 'open strong enhancer' regions (Figure 5B), such that their reweighted PPAs rose to 21% (rs10771372), 21% (rs10842992) and 13% (rs10842991), respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Allelic imbalance was observed only at rs10842991 at the KLHDC5 locus, with the T2D-risk C allele showing greater chromatin accessibility (binomial p=4.1×10−3).
source: We observed allelic imbalance only at rs10842991 with the T2D-risk C allele showing greater chromatin accessibility (binomial p=4.1×10−3, Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the allelic imbalance analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: rs10842991 overlapped a predicted TFBS motif for PAX6.
source: This variant further overlapped a predicted TFBS motif for PAX6 as determined by the software tool FIMO (Grant et al., 2011): the T2D-risk allele was predicted to enhance PAX6 transcription factor binding consistent with the allelic effects on increasing chromatin accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis, with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: The T2D-risk allele of rs10842991 was predicted to enhance PAX6 transcription factor binding.
source: This variant further overlapped a predicted TFBS motif for PAX6 as determined by the software tool FIMO (Grant et al., 2011): the T2D-risk allele was predicted to enhance PAX6 transcription factor binding consistent with the allelic effects on increasing chromatin accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis, with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: The strong enhancer region containing rs10842991 is almost exclusively found in islets, with strong enhancer H3K27ac states overlapping rs10842991 in only two non-islet tissues out of 99 tissues.
source: This strong enhancer region is almost exclusively found in islets, with strong enhancer H3K27ac states overlapping rs10842991 in only two non-islet (heart and smooth muscle) Epigenome Roadmap tissues (out of 99 tissues with 18-state chromatin state information, Figure 5B)(Kundaje et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from comparison with Epigenome Roadmap data, with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Islet eQTL data links rs10842991 and close proxy SNPs to islet transcription with the risk allele increasing KLHDC5 expression.
source: Islet eQTL data (Varshney et al., 2017) also links rs10842991 and close proxy SNPs (including rs7960190) to islet transcription with the risk allele increasing KLHDC5 expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: rs10842991 is the likely causal variant at the KLHDC5 T2D GWAS locus.
source: These data prioritise rs10842991 as the likely causal variant at the KLHDC5 T2D GWAS locus, and indicate a likely molecular mechanism involving modified PAX6 transcription factor binding and an impact on KLHDC5 expression and islet function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of multiple lines of evidence.

claim: At the ADCY5 locus, reweighting of variants based on epigenomic annotation clearly prioritised variant rs11708067 (PPA = 92%).
source: The third example of allelic imbalance mapped to the ADCY5 locus. Fine-mapping based solely on genetic data could not prioritise a distinct causal variant due to multiple variants in high LD (range for top five variants = 12–26%, Figure 5C). However, reweighting of variants based on epigenomic annotation clearly prioritised variant rs11708067: this SNP overlapped an 'open weak enhancer' and captured most of the reweighted PPA (PPA = 92%).
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: At rs11708067, the T2D-risk A allele was associated with decreased chromatin accessibility (binomial p=1.2×10−6).
source: Allelic imbalance analysis also showed that the T2D-risk A allele was associated with decreased chromatin accessibility (binomial p=1.2×10−6, Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the allelic imbalance analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: rs11708067 maps to an islet cis-eQTL and methylation QTL at which the T2D-risk allele is associated with reduced ADCY5 expression and increased ADCY5 gene body DNA methylation.
source: The same lead variant maps to an islet cis-eQTL and methylation QTL (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) at which the T2D-risk allele is associated with reduced ADCY5 expression and increased ADCY5 gene body DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a result from the study's analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Capture-C confirmed physical contact between the ADCY5 promoter and the hypomethylated open chromatin enhancer region harbouring rs11708067.
source: To further understand the role of the rs11708067 variant, we performed ATAC-seq and Next Generation Capture-C, in the glucose-responsive human beta-cell line EndoC-βH1 (n = 3). We targeted the ADCY5 promoter to define distal regions interacting with the promoter, and confirmed physical contact with the hypomethylated open chromatin enhancer region harbouring rs11708067 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the Capture-C experiment, with reference to figures.

claim: After adjusting for multiple testing using FDR correction, only two fragments yielded a significant normalised read number over background in the Capture-C analysis at ADCY5, including the fragment containing rs11708067.
source: To resolve the significance of the interaction between the restriction fragment encompassing rs11708067 and the ADCY5 promoter, we used the programme peakC (de Wit and Geeven, 2017) (https://github.com/deWitLab/peakC) to evaluate the interactions of 12 fragments covering the lead SNP rs11708067 and 15 SNPs in high LD (r2 >0.8) across a region of 47 kb. After adjusting for multiple testing using FDR correction, only two fragments yielded a significant normalised read number over background. This included the open-chromatin overlapping fragment containing rs11708067 and another fragment harbouring rs2877716, rs6798189, rs56371916 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the Capture-C analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: rs11708067 is the likely causal variant affecting islet accessible chromatin at the ADCY5 locus.
source: These findings support rs11708067 as the likely causal variant affecting islet accessible chromatin (in line with another recent study [Roman et al., 2017]), and link the open and hypomethylated enhancer element in which it sits to regulation of ADCY5 expression in islets.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of multiple lines of evidence and supported by a citation.

claim: The present study describes genome-wide patterns of methylation and chromatin accessibility in human islet material in unprecedented detail.
source: The present study seeks to address this deficit by describing, in unprecedented detail, genome-wide patterns of methylation and chromatin accessibility in human islet material.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution.

claim: The refined regulatory map offers more granular annotation of functional impact based on improved enrichment for T2D association signals.
source: We have combined these data with existing islet epigenomic marks to generate a refined regulatory map which, based on the evidence of improved enrichment for T2D association signals, offers more granular annotation of functional impact.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution based on the enrichment analyses.

claim: The integrative analysis of T2D GWAS and epigenetic data has enabled a detailed and comprehensive analysis that considers the regulatory impact of all variants at CDC123 and ADCY5 loci across multiple islet samples.
source: While previous studies had explored the candidacy of selected variants at the CDC123 (Fogarty et al., 2014) and ADCY5 (Olsson et al., 2014; Hodson et al., 2014; van de Bunt et al., 2015) loci with respect to islet regulation and T2D predisposition, our integrative analysis of T2D GWAS and epigenetic data has enabled a detailed and comprehensive analysis that considers the regulatory impact of all variants at these loci across multiple islet samples.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution compared to prior work, with citations.

claim: The findings at ADCY5 are supported by a recent paper that found allelic imbalance in H3K27 acetylation involving the rs11708067 variant in a single human islet sample.
source: The findings at ADCY5 are supported by a recent paper that found allelic imbalance in H3K27 acetylation involving the rs11708067 variant in a single human islet sample, and which observed that deletion of the relevant enhancer element led to reduction in both ADCY5 gene expression and insulin secretion (Roman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The integrative approach provides useful insights into the functional mechanisms through which T2D GWAS signals operate.
source: Overall, our integrative approach provides useful insights into the functional mechanisms through which T2D GWAS signals operate.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution.

claim: Only a small minority of dDMRs overlap functional islet regulatory regions.
source: The whole genome methylation data generated in the present study also allowed us to evaluate the likely contribution of previously identified T2D-associated dDMRs (Volkov et al., 2017) with respect to T2D predisposition. These dDMRs, defined on the basis of observed differences in methylation between islets recovered from diabetic and non-diabetic donors, cover a substantial part of the genome, but we were able to show that only a small minority of these overlap functional islet regulatory regions.
evidence: This is a result from the study's analysis of dDMRs.

claim: dDMR regions as a whole had no significant enrichment for T2D association signals.
source: As a consequence, dDMR regions as a whole had no significant enrichment for T2D association signals.
evidence: This is a result from the FGWAS analysis of dDMRs.

claim: Most of the dDMR signal involves stochastic effects and/or the secondary consequences on methylation of the diabetic state.
source: This suggests that most of the dDMR signal involves stochastic effects and/or the secondary consequences on methylation of the diabetic state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of enrichment for T2D association signals.

claim: The FGWAS approach is limited in its ability to determine the effect of multiple variants at individual loci.
source: Although we provide highly detailed functional fine-mapping of T2D genetic variants to uncover causal variants, the FGWAS approach applied in this study is limited in its ability to determine the effect of multiple variants at individual loci.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the method used.

claim: FGWAS relies on the assumption of a single causal variant within each region, which may not necessarily be true for all loci.
source: Specifically, FGWAS relies on the assumption of a single causal variant within each region, which may not necessarily be true for all loci.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions and limitations of the method used.

claim: The power to detect allelic imbalance in chromatin accessibility was restricted to sites with common variants and relatively large effects.
source: In addition, while the present study characterises islet epigenome status and variability in chromatin accessibility in substantially larger numbers of islet samples than those previously reported (Gaulton et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2013; Pasquali et al., 2014; Varshney et al., 2017), the number of islet preparations for which these data were available was still limited. As a result, our power to detect allelic imbalance in chromatin accessibility was restricted to sites with common variants and relatively large effects.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The genomic data was generated only from islet samples from non-diabetic donors.
source: A further limitation is that the genomic data we analysed was generated only from islet samples from non-diabetic donors.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.
